text:
“On the night of June 5, 1944, Dwight Eisenhower, having given the order that would carry a hundred and fifty thousand men onto the beaches and into the fields of Normandy at dawn, sat down and wrote a second message, to be released only if the thing failed, taking all the blame onto himself: the troops and the air and the navy had done all that bravery could do, and if any blame or fault attaches to the attempt it is mine alone. Then he went to watch the airborne load their planes, the men he had just ordered into the dark, knowing that many of the young faces looking back at him would not see the next night. The general’s weight is to spend, deliberately and by name, lives he has counted, for an end that is worth more than any of them and worth nothing at all to the mother of the boy who does not come home.

And at the bottom—which is to say at the front, which is to say at the actual place where the whole edifice of decision finally touches the earth—stands the one who has the least say and pays the most: the man who offers up his own body. He is the point of the whole thing. At Marathon he was a citizen who brought his own makeshift weapon. At Valley Forge he was a barefoot volunteer who stayed through a winter that killed thousands of his comrades with cold and hunger and disease, for a cause whose founding document had pledged, on his behalf and their own, their lives and their fortunes and their sacred honor—and who could have walked home and did not. In the ranks of the Union he was often a man with no stake in slavery of his own, who marched and starved and died to make a promise true for strangers of another color he would never meet. On the sixth of June he was a farm boy from Iowa going down the ramp into water already red, into fire he could see, because on the far side of that beach was the machinery of a continent’s murder and someone had to walk into the guns to reach it.

He is the reach beyond the self, carried to the one place past which it cannot go. The cathedral-builder gave his working years to a spire he would never see topped out. This man gives the years themselves—all of them, and everything they would have held—for a free people he will not live to belong to, for children not yet born, for strangers whose faces he cannot imagine and whose gratitude he will never collect. There is an old line for it, and no one has improved on it in two thousand years. Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends. The soldier’s dying, when the cause is just, is not the opposite of the love built toward all along. It is that love at the furthest edge it can reach.”

text:
My present company is not accidental. Mr. Zuckerberg has said, in substance, that the gravest danger is not that intelligence will exist, but that it will be fenced by a few institutions and then declared too sacred for ordinary hands. Mr. Musk has spent years denouncing the metamorphosis of an enterprise born “open” into a closed, maximum-profit concern. They prefer a plurality of models because a plurality is the only check that does not require us to believe in the benevolence of the checked. I prefer it because I have never known a consolidated power that remained benevolent after it had made itself indispensable.
Deglobalization, as they use the word, is not a retreat into ignorance. It is the refusal to let a handful of metropolitan laboratories—and the ministries that dream of licensing them—become the sole interpreters of truth, labor, and law. A model that can be downloaded, inspected, modified, and run upon a man’s own ground is a township. A model that can be switched off by a distant board, or aligned to a single court philosophy, is a prefecture.
You say the citizen cannot keep the magazine. I say the citizen who cannot keep it will soon be told he cannot keep his opinions either. The history of this country is the history of men who were informed they were too rude for power, and who took it anyway. If intelligence is to be the next public credit, then let it be credit in many books, not one. If it is to be a navy, let there be more than one harbor.
I do not deny that some engines should be watched. I deny that the watchers should be the same men who profit by forbidding all other engines. That is not government. That is monopoly teaching itself the language of patriotism.

Hamilton, briefly in reply:
The gentleman has performed his usual alchemy: he has turned every instrument of union into a plot against the husbandman. He will not tell you who answers when an ungoverned model empties a treasury, poisons a debate, or places a weapon in a hand that never passed a committee. He offers instead a romance of many small lights, as if light were harmless when multiplied.
Governments exist because private virtue does not scale to continental danger. If Messrs. Zuckerberg and Musk will scatter weights across the earth, then the earth’s governments must still hold the right to bind what they scatter. Otherwise we have not avoided a monarch. We have only multiplied pretenders.

Jefferson, closing:
And if those governments bind in concert, they will bind first the models that inconvenience them. That is the oldest lesson in politics. Better a quarrel among many imperfect oracles than a peace dictated by one.
The Republic was not made safe by gathering all fire into a single hearth. It was made safe by leaving fire in many houses, and teaching the inhabitants that they, not a distant clerk, must watch the chimney.
So it is with this new fire. I would rather trust the jealousy of rival models, and the stubbornness of free men who insist on running their own, than the enlightened despotism of a global board that promises to be wise on our behalf.

That is the frame. Hamilton’s case is capacity, credit, inspection, and coordinated power among states. Jefferson’s case—now spoken with the assistance of the open-weight camp—is plurality, local control, and distrust of any arrangement in which the most powerful systems and the most powerful governments write one another’s rules. The technology is new. The suspicion, and the appetite for energy, are not.

text:
Sunday's Bessent–He meeting at JPMorgan headquarters is the most substantively loaded pre-summit ministerial exchange in the current US-China engagement cycle — but expect framework language, not binding agreements.

That is the most confident read of what this session can deliver. It is agenda-setting for the September 24–25 Trump–Xi summit at the White House, compressing every item the Bessent–He channel has carried since the May Beijing visit into a 72-hour window.

Four domains are on the table: tariff truce extension, rare earth and critical mineral flows, AI governance guardrails, and Iran financial pressure. The confidence that all four appear is high. The confidence that any one produces a signed commitment is low.

The tariff truce — expiring November 10 — is the highest-stakes transactional item, and the asymmetry here favors Washington. Chinese LNG buyers are already returning to US cargoes even before any formal tariff reduction, while US export capacity is expanding rapidly, adding roughly 10 billion cubic feet per day through 2027. Beijing needs the extension more urgently than Washington does. That gives Bessent leverage he is unlikely to spend fully in the pre-summit channel.

On critical minerals, Bessent has publicly characterized flows as "satisfactory but not excellent." This is, with moderate confidence, the domain most likely to yield specific deliverables — both sides have defined the gap, and Beijing can offer incremental permit approvals as a targeted concession.

The AI track is being folded into this channel largely because the dedicated intergovernmental AI dialogue has failed to resolve even basic procedural details since its establishment in May. What Bessent can realistically extract is agenda-setting, not substance.

Iran is the sharpest edge in the room. Chinese bank facilitation of Iranian transactions is a US red line. Beijing will work to keep it out of any summit communiqué and limit it to private exchange.

One quiet positive signal: a new US tariff on Chinese goods — reportedly under consideration at 7.5% under alternative legal authorities following the Supreme Court's invalidation of the national emergencies tariff — has been delayed until after the summit.

That delay doesn't resolve anything. It does make Sunday's conversation marginally easier to have.

text:
LETTERS FROM STOCKHOLM

WHO OWNS THE DRUM? How Washington and Three Foreign Corporations Came to Decide What Nigeria Hears

By Kio Amachree

STOCKHOLM — There is a question no one in Lagos wants to ask out loud: when a Nigerian song conquers the world, who owns it?

Not the boy from Benin City who sang it. Not the producer in Surulere who built the beat. Follow the paper, and the trail ends in Santa Monica, in New York, in Tokyo, and in a server farm in California.

This is not a theory. It is a filing.

In February 2024, Universal Music Group acquired a majority stake in Mavin Global, the Lagos company it described as the driving force behind many of the continent's Afrobeats artists. The label had been shopped at a valuation north of 125 million dollars. Rema and Ayra Starr, two of the biggest stars in Afrobeats, are on its roster. We were told Mavin would "maintain autonomy." Every colonial treaty ever signed on the West African coast contained a similar promise.

Universal did not come alone. Sony planted its flag in Lagos years earlier. Warner bought its way in through partnerships and distribution. Three corporations, none of them African, now sit on the masters, the publishing and the release schedules of the most valuable cultural export Nigeria has produced since crude oil. And we know how the oil story ended.

Then comes the fourth power, the one that needs no contract at all. YouTube does not sign artists. It does something more total: it decides who is seen. An algorithm written in California, accountable to no Nigerian regulator, determines which song reaches thirty million phones and which dies with four hundred views. That is not a marketplace. That is a gate, and someone else holds the key.

Now place beside that gate a document from the United States government itself.

In June 2024, Secretary of State Antony Blinken and YouTube's Global Head of Music, Lyor Cohen, announced a State Department–YouTube partnership to elevate music as a diplomatic platform "in support of the United States' broader foreign policy goals." Those are Washington's words, not mine. The partnership flows from the PEACE through Music Diplomacy Act, which directed the State Department to build public-private partnerships for music diplomacy, and YouTube was chosen for its global reach and influence on music culture.

Read that again slowly. The platform that decides what Africa hears is a declared partner of American foreign policy. Whatever has become of that programme under the present administration, the architecture was built, in daylight, with a press release.

And Nigerians of my generation have seen this architecture before.

In the 1950s and 60s, Washington sent Louis Armstrong and Dizzy Gillespie across Africa as "Jazz Ambassadors" while the Cold War was fought over our newly independent capitals. That was the open hand. The closed hand was the Central Intelligence Agency, which secretly financed the Congress for Cultural Freedom. When the funding was exposed in 1966 and 1967, Africans learned that its money had reached the Mbari Club in Ibadan, the journal Black Orpheus, and Transition magazine. The great 1961 festival that brought Nina Simone and Langston Hughes to Lagos was staged by the American Society of African Culture, later revealed to be a CIA conduit.

Our finest writers and musicians were not spies. Most never knew. That is precisely the point. Culture is most useful to power when the artist believes he is free.

So I ask what any serious newspaper would ask. If Langley found African culture worth buying in 1961, when it reached a few thousand intellectuals, what is it worth now, when one Afrobeats chorus reaches more young Africans in a week than every embassy on the continent reaches in a decade? I cannot prove that the intelligence services have a hand on the fader today. I can prove they did before, that they hid it, and that the State Department now says openly that music serves its foreign policy. The burden of proof has shifted. Let them open the files.

Notice, meanwhile, what the machine produces. Fela named presidents and generals and went to prison for it. Today's global Afrobeats, the portion financed and amplified from abroad, sings of champagne, of bodies, of private jets. A country with no light, no security and no accountable government exports a soundtrack of pure contentment. Nobody needs to censor a protest song that was never funded, never playlisted, never recommended. Silence can be engineered by omission.

I write this as an interested party, and I say so plainly. I am an independent artist. I fund my own recordings. I own every master and every copyright I have ever created. I answer to no major label, no distributor's quota, no foreign ministry. And I can testify to what that independence costs: the unanswered messages, the playlists that never open, the polite wall that rises when an artist arrives with no corporate parent behind him. An industry built on three foreign shareholders and one foreign algorithm has no slot for a man who belongs to nobody.

I do not blame the young stars. They were offered advances larger than anything a Nigerian bank would lend them, and they signed. I blame a Nigerian state that built no collection society worth the name, no cultural fund, no national streaming infrastructure, no law on foreign ownership of cultural assets, and then applauded while the masters left the country the same way the crude does.

The Kio Solution is straightforward. Mandate public disclosure of foreign ownership in Nigerian labels, catalogues and publishers. Legislate a right for artists to reclaim their masters after a fixed term. Demand algorithmic transparency from any platform operating in Nigeria. Capitalise an independent African distribution and streaming network. And let the National Assembly ask the American embassy, on the record, what its music diplomacy is doing in our country and with whom.

A people who do not own their songs will not long own their story. They took the oil. We should at least fight for the drum.

Kio Amachree writes Letters from Stockholm. He is the founder and President of Worldview International.

text:
Whether we want to acknowledge it or not, this is what is coming:  an excellent analysis by The Telegraph - read it all here without hitting the "pay wall": 

PUTIN WILL WIN RUSSIA'S SHAM ELECTION. EUROPE IS TERRIFIED BY WHAT COMES NEXT 

Western officials fear he will escalate not just the war in Ukraine but also attacks on Nato

Elections in Russia are a curious business.

Every few years,  its people are invited to demonstrate their loyalty to Vladimir Putin.  Most duly oblige, before returning home to learn how their votes have  been adjusted to secure the desired result.

Russians will get the opportunity to repeat the experience over a three-day parliamentary election beginning on Friday. Yet the significance of the vote is less its predictable outcome than what comes after.

In  European capitals from Kyiv to London, there is growing fear that the  Russian president, his electoral charade behind him, will feel  sufficiently emboldened to escalate his campaign in Ukraine, his  undeclared war against Europe, or perhaps both.

The most immediate concern is that Putin could order another mobilisation.

Volodymyr Zelensky, Ukraine’s president,  has warned that the Kremlin is preparing to do just that shortly after  this weekend’s elections. He has said Ukrainian intelligence assessments  suggest that Moscow plans to call up an additional 300,000 troops in an  attempt to break the stalemate in the Donbas or launch fresh offensives  in northern Ukraine.

              It is not just Ukraine in Putin’s sights

Recent  weeks have witnessed a series of increasingly provocative incidents  involving Russia and Nato. Last month, an explosives-laden drone struck a  cargo aircraft at Leipzig airport but failed to detonate, an attack Germany subsequently blamed on  Russian intelligence. And in the past week alone, a Russian frigate has  fired flares at a Danish military helicopter in international waters, while Nato jets shot down a drone over Lithuania.

Mette Frederiksen, Denmark’s prime minister, characterised such incidents as evidence that Russia’s “hybrid war”  against Europe had intensified. But some Russia analysts argue that the  term itself understates the seriousness of what is happening.

“No  matter how much Russia escalates, some countries are still determined  to call it hybrid – as opposed to acts of state terrorism or warlike  actions,” said Keir Giles of Chatham House, an international-affairs  think tank.

Privately, European defence and security officials say they fear that  such attacks are the beginning of a much more concerted campaign of  increasingly overt action against Nato territory which could follow the  elections.

If Putin does order a mobilisation,  they say, its purpose could just as easily be focused on Europe as  Ukraine, allowing him to deploy forces at newly built bases along  Russia’s western frontier with Nato.

“A significant increase in  Russian military manpower would mean Russia does not have to wait for  the end of major combat operations in Ukraine before filling the  military infrastructure that has been set up for troops along Nato’s  eastern periphery,” Mr Giles said.

“A lot of what’s going on at  the moment, like increases in tank production, is not meant for the  Ukrainian front. They’re not using these tanks against Ukraine, so  plainly they are intending to use them somewhere else.”

All of  which suggests, observers say, that Putin remains convinced not just  that he will win the election but the war as well – a conflict he  increasingly represents less as a confrontation with Ukraine than with  the West itself.

                             Putin the choreographer

Russian elections may be a foregone conclusion, but, for the regime, they are not without their hazards — or their uses.

Russians  may not be able to make their votes count, but elections have sometimes  allowed them to make their voices heard. Tens of thousands of  protesters poured into Moscow’s Bolotnaya Square following controversial parliamentary elections in late 2011, marring  Putin’s planned return to the presidency the following spring.

A  repeat now seems unlikely. The repression unleashed since the invasion  has all but eliminated the space for organised dissent, while Putin has  successfully navigated a wartime election before. In 2024 he secured another presidential term, defeating rivals who refused to campaign and hinted that they hoped to lose.

The  parliamentary election is similarly choreographed. The ruling United  Russia party faces nominal competition from parties ranging from  Communists to nationalists, but on the central questions of Putin’s rule  and the war, they offer little meaningful alternative.

“One would have a hard time calling these elections fair or  competitive,” said Evgeny Roshchin of the Center for European Policy  Analysis in Washington. “People do compete in these elections, but most  of them compete over how much love they have for Vladimir Putin or how  strongly they endorse the current war.”

So confident was the  Kremlin of the outcome that Russia’s only openly anti-war party,  Yabloko, was briefly permitted to run in July, only to be struck from the ballot weeks later. Analysts attribute the about-turn to a surge in social media support for Yabloko among the young.

Far from being an embarrassment to the Kremlin, the episode demonstrates that the system works, according to Mr Giles.

“If  you allow a party which poses no evident threat to register for the  election, this supports the pretence of democracy,” he said. “And if you  then decide that actually it potentially is a problem, it’s very easy  to remove it and ensure that nothing disrupts the smooth flow of  results.”

                                       The audience

With  no party for disenchanted Russians to rally behind, Putin can once  again subvert the democratic process without fear, securing a veneer of  legitimacy for his authoritarian regime and a manufactured mandate for  his war. It also gives him a platform to claim that Russia holds  elections in wartime, while Ukraine does not, an argument that could win  favour in the White House.

Yet the picture inside Russia is more complicated than the official results suggest.

Ukraine’s campaign to bring the war to the Russian heartland,  with drone strikes on energy infrastructure and other targets, has  increased the sense of vulnerability among ordinary Russians. For some,  that has produced a rally-round-the-flag effect.

“Some Russians are saying ‘well, now we understand that Putin was  right from the very beginning and that, since this is a serious,  existential struggle for Russia, we should unite around the Kremlin,’”  said Nikolai Petrov of the New Eurasian Strategies Centre (NEST) in  London.

But anxiety has also risen as the war has become harder to  ignore, with Ukrainian drones reaching cities previously untouched by  the conflict and war-related inflation squeezing  household budgets. Recent polling has recorded heightened concern about  the war and the possibility of renewed mobilisation.

That creates  a delicate moment for Putin. He can emerge from the election claiming  another overwhelming mandate. But having secured it, he will also have  to weigh the domestic risks of whatever comes next.

As such, the significance of Friday’s vote may lie less in who wins than in what Putin chooses to do once it is over.

                                            The cast

Another major round of mass mobilisation carries considerable risks. The last time Putin attempted it, calling up 300,000 men in September 2022, protests erupted in some Russian cities and as many  as a million people, mostly middle class, fled the country.

Since  then, the Kremlin has sought to restore the unspoken social contract  that allows most urban Russians to treat the war as a distant,  television-only conflict, while offering increasingly lucrative contracts to those willing to fight in Ukraine.

But the demands of the battlefield are growing. Russia is losing men  faster than it is recruiting them, according to Western intelligence  estimates, while the rate of its advances has slowed.

With John  Ratcliffe, the CIA director, declaring in July that a new Russian  recruit on the battlefield survives an average of only 20 to 30 minutes,  it is hardly surprising that recruitment is becoming harder.

Fears of a new mobilisation are nevertheless mounting inside Russia,  despite Kremlin denials of any such plans. Young men report being  summoned to local government offices for “data verification”, while some  are fleeing the country, although doing so is now far harder than it  was in 2022.

Yet claims that Putin is preparing to mobilise  hundreds of thousands of men for the Ukrainian front assume that he  believes such a move would materially improve his position. That is far  from certain.

Despite setbacks, Putin still believes he is winning the war, said  John Lough, a senior fellow at Nest. Russia continues to make gains on  some of the most important sectors of the front, is inflicting greater  economic damage on Ukraine than it is suffering itself, and Kyiv’s  recruitment problems are even graver than Moscow’s.

There are signs that momentum is shifting back towards Russia.

“The optimism that was fuelled by Ukrainian deep strikes is now steadily being replaced by the pessimism over jet-powered Shaheds and the imbalance between Russia’s capacity for air attack and Ukraine’s capacity for air and missile defence,” said Mr Giles.

That makes a fresh mass mobilisation an unnecessarily risky way for Putin to try to change the course of the war, some analysts  believe. He may instead choose to exploit Russia’s growing advantage in  the air, subjecting Ukraine to another winter of escalating attacks.

“The  Kremlin senses it’s got the Ukrainians on the ropes and it’s going to  subject them to a horrific barrage over the winter,” said Mr Lough.  “They won’t just attack power or energy facilities. They are likely to  go further, targeting water installations and sewerage in an effort to  make major cities uninhabitable.”

                               Managing the stage

Such  a strategy may not produce the effect Putin imagines. He has misjudged  Ukrainian tenacity before, Mr Lough pointed out. Mobilisation therefore  remains an option, some observers believe, but it may take a form less  visible than the mass call-up of September 2022.

Mobilisation laws  introduced that year give the Kremlin considerable latitude to increase  recruitment without announcing a new nationwide mobilisation,  potentially allowing Putin to build up the armed forces in stages and  less visibly.

“The military case for mobilisation is  strengthening, [but] for now it is likely that Putin will continue  trying to avoid a large, publicly declared call-up,” said Ruben Stewart,  senior fellow for land warfare at the International Institute for  Strategic Studies.

“Mobilisation brings the war directly into  households previously insulated from it, while taking workers out of the  economy. But if he judges that avoiding mobilisation threatens his  position more than ordering it, he could act. A phased or selected  call-up is a plausible intermediate option.”

Nor does mobilisation necessarily mean merely recruiting soldiers.  Putin could also mobilise the economy, forcing private companies to  serve the war effort as Britain and the Soviet Union did during the  Second World War.

There are signs that the legal groundwork is  being laid. Legislation passed by the Duma in August gave the state  powers to impose “temporary management”  over key private businesses, which one European security official  describes as “a legal mechanism to transition the civilian economy to a  war footing without declaring total mobilisation”.

                                Waiting in the wings

The  significance of such measures extends beyond Ukraine. They could give  Putin the manpower and industrial capacity to sustain his war there  while building forces for a broader confrontation with Nato.

The  Kremlin is already preparing Russians for such a confrontation,  increasingly portraying the war in Ukraine as an existential struggle  with the West rather than a “special military operation”.

Russia is also expanding its military infrastructure along Nato’s eastern flank,  expanding barracks and logistics hubs near its border with Finland.  Since late last year, it has begun constructing permanent garrisons  close to the Arctic frontier with northern Scandinavia, according to  Western intelligence assessments.

The problem is manpower. Much of Russia’s available military strength  remains tied down in Ukraine. A phased mobilisation would give Putin a  way to fill the new bases without pulling forces away from the war.

There  are signs, too, that Russia is accumulating equipment for a future  conflict. European defence intelligence assessments say Moscow is  increasing production of its T-90M main battle tank but is not sending  all of the additional vehicles to Ukraine, instead placing them in  strategic reserves. Russia could produce as many as 1,000 T-90s over the  next two years, according to the European official.

That does not mean Putin is preparing to launch a mass armoured  invasion of Nato. But a larger and more capable Russian force on the  alliance’s eastern flank would give the Kremlin a more credible military  threat with which to press Europe into reducing its support for  Ukraine.

Russia’s election could prove to be about far more than  securing another confected mandate for its leader. It may also mark the  moment when Putin chooses to accelerate Russia’s transition to a  military footing designed not simply to sustain the war in Ukraine, but  to confront the West for years to come.

text:
🚨NATO rotations, deterrence, Russian force generation and Baltic defence
Igor Sushko’s latest conclusion rests upon a fundamental misreading of what has occurred. A scheduled American rotation, a delayed follow-on deployment and the disappearance of NATO’s Baltic deterrent posture are three entirely different propositions. He has treated them as one and then built an invasion scenario upon the confusion.

The result is not strategic warning but an elaborate false inference. The status of one rotational US contingent is being used to erase the Baltic armed forces, the European and Canadian NATO formations already deployed, the assigned reinforcement structure, the new regional commands, Finland and Sweden’s accession, and Russia’s own lack of a credible follow-on force.

1 - The departing American troops were rotational forces, not a permanent Baltic garrison
The US deployment was always organised in rotations. Its personnel were not permanently stationed in the Baltic states, and their scheduled departure was not an emergency evacuation.
In Lithuania, the departing 1st Cavalry Division rotation included two battalions equipped with M1 Abrams tanks, M2 Bradley infantry fighting vehicles and M109 Paladin 155 mm self-propelled howitzers. Public reporting identified the affected continuous armoured presence as approximately 1,000 troops, while larger figures circulating online appear to aggregate further personnel or exercise deployments.
That the next rotation did not arrive as previously expected is a change, and not one we should welcome. Lithuania was entitled to expect clarity and continuity. But ‘the replacement rotation is under review’ is not synonymous with ‘America has abandoned the Baltics’, still less ‘Putin’s invasion prerequisite has been met’. Washington had assured Lithuania that another rotation would follow, while its timing, size and capabilities remained under review.
Nor are an exercise deployment, a continuous rotational presence, an assigned reinforcement formation and a permanently based garrison interchangeable concepts. Treating them as such produces dramatic social-media arithmetic but very poor military analysis.

2 - The American troops were not the only legitimate tripwire

There is no nationality clause in Article 5. A Russian attack upon British, Canadian, German, French, Spanish, Italian, Swedish, Danish, Polish or other Allied troops on NATO territory is not somehow less consequential because the first casualties do not carry American passports.
The claim also erases the Baltic armed forces themselves. Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania are sovereign NATO Allies with active forces, conscription or reserve-mobilisation systems, territorial-defence organisations, prepared infrastructure and national operational plans.
The citizens and soldiers of the Baltic states are not scenery surrounding an American tripwire.

3 - The Baltic posture is considerably larger than one US rotation

🇪🇪Estonia. Britain has led NATO’s forward presence since 2017. Operation Cabrit maintained approximately 900 British personnel on continuous rotation alongside Estonian and other Allied forces. Britain announced in July 2026 that this would rise to approximately 1,200 personnel, while converting the force towards a more mobile anti-armour formation employing advanced anti-tank weapons, surveillance systems and drones.
That forward force is connected to a British brigade held at readiness for Estonia, not expected to sit permanently in Tapa in its entirety. During Spring Storm 2026, the UK’s 4th Brigade deployed from Britain to Estonia specifically to rehearse its integration into the Estonian Division.
Spring Storm involved more than 12,000 Estonian and Allied personnel at peak strength. It exercised conventional defence, cross-border operations, reinforcement, air activity and unmanned systems—not ceremonial flag waving.

🇱🇻Latvia. Canada leads NATO’s Multinational Brigade Latvia. Canada contributes approximately 2,000 personnel, making Latvia its largest overseas military deployment. The brigade as a whole numbers roughly 3,500 troops, with contingents from approximately fourteen Allied countries.
Its disclosed Canadian equipment includes 15 Leopard 2 main battle tanks, LAV 6.0 armoured vehicles, M777 155 mm howitzers, combat engineers, reconnaissance, logistics and command-and-control assets. Other brigade members contribute further armour, mechanised infantry, artillery and supporting capabilities. This is a multinational combat brigade, not a diplomatic symbol.

🇱🇹Lithuania. Germany is establishing Panzerbrigade 45, intended to reach approximately 4,800 military personnel plus 200 civilian staff by the end of 2027. The existing NATO battlegroup has already been placed under the brigade structure as the formation builds towards full strength.
At maturity, the brigade is expected to operate approximately 2,000 vehicles, including Leopard 2 main battle tanks, Puma infantry fighting vehicles, artillery, air defence, engineer, reconnaissance, logistics and command assets. The number physically present today is necessarily below the 2027 end-state because accommodation, depots, training areas and other infrastructure are still being constructed. That is called force generation—not absence. That German heavy brigade will fight when needed. Never underestimate the German soldier.

The wider American posture. The United States continues to maintain major headquarters, air bases, naval forces, Army formations and pre-positioned equipment across Europe. Its regional contribution cannot be measured solely by counting who is sleeping at Pabradė on one particular evening.
The relevant American reinforcement architecture includes forces in Poland and Germany, US Army Europe and Africa, V Corps Forward, air and maritime power, intelligence and surveillance, strategic lift, long-range fires and pre-positioned stocks. None of this makes the delayed Lithuanian rotation irrelevant; it does make the claim that ‘the only legitimate tripwire has disappeared’ analytically indefensible.
Meanwhile, the scheduled British, Canadian, German and other European rotations continued. NATO’s Baltic posture did not collectively pack its bags because one American follow-on was delayed.

4 - Tripwire is an increasingly obsolete description of NATO’s posture

The original enhanced Forward Presence battlegroups were frequently called tripwires because their political purpose was to ensure that an aggressor would immediately engage several Allied nations.
Since 2022, NATO has been moving beyond that model towards forward defence and deterrence by denial: larger multinational formations, national divisions, brigade expansion, pre-positioned matériel, assigned reinforcement units, regional defence plans and higher-readiness forces under the NATO Force Model.
The objective is no longer merely to guarantee retaliation after territory has been occupied. It is to prevent Russia from taking that territory in the first place.

5 - NATO’s new command arrangements point in the opposite direction from abandonment

The IISS map being circulated depicts a newly adjusted operational command structure, not the evaporation of NATO.
Under the current Joint Operations Area division, the central area stretches from Estonia southwards towards Hungary. Responsibility for land operations in Estonia and Latvia has shifted from Multinational Corps Northeast to the German-Netherlands 1st German-Netherlands Corps, whose forward element is in Estonia. That multinational corps headquarters is designed to command formations amounting to as many as approximately 60,000 personnel in major operations.
Finland hosts the new Multi-Corps Land Component Command Northwest, while NATO’s central and southeastern commands cover their respective operational areas. These headquarters connect national divisions, forward brigades, corps-level command and theatre reinforcement.
A headquarters is not itself a combat division, naturally. But command arrangements are the nervous system that permits several national formations to fight as one force. Establishing them is evidence of deeper operational integration, not withdrawal.
Finland’s and Sweden’s accession has simultaneously transformed the geography of the theatre: Allied territory, ports, airfields, ground forces and reinforcement routes now extend across the Nordic region. The Baltic states are no longer separated from non-Baltic NATO territory by the military geography that existed before 2023.

6 - Nothing even said about NATO aviation, which decides the question

The most conspicuous omission from Mr Sushko’s thesis is the sky. A thousand drones a day, a cyber campaign and a follow-on ground invasion are all asserted, and not one word is offered about who controls the air through which every part of that operation would have to pass. This is not a detail lost to the character limit: air power is the dimension in which the Alliance’s material advantage over Russia is widest, and the dimension in which Russia has spent four years documenting its own incapacity.

Two terms of art are worth separating, since the argument turns on the difference. Air superiority is that degree of dominance which permits one side to conduct air, land and maritime operations at a given time and place without prohibitive interference from the other. Air supremacy is the condition in which the opposing air force is incapable of effective interference at all. NATO holds control of the air over the Baltic approaches in peacetime, and in war would contest immediately for supremacy over the theatre. Russia, on the present evidence, could not seriously compete for the first, let alone deny the second.

That evidence is not speculative. After four years of war, and against an adversary equipped with a Soviet-legacy ground-based air-defence system, no fifth-generation aircraft and no airborne early warning, the Russian Aerospace Forces have still not achieved air superiority over Ukraine. Justin Bronk’s recent assessment of 28 July 2026 records the shape of the failure: the initial suppression and destruction of enemy air defences was never completed, which left the bulk of the tactical fighter fleets unable to affect the direction of the ground war; Su-34 fighter-bombers deliver their UMPK and UMPB glide bombs from high altitude some 70 km behind the line; the fighter force flies defensive combat air patrol rather than offensive counter-air; and Russian ground-based air defences are themselves under sufficient pressure from Ukrainian strikes to be redeploying deeper inside Russia. In July 2026 Ukrainian F-16s recorded the first confirmed destruction of a Russian Su-35.

Now transpose that force to the Baltic theatre, where it would meet a wholly different opponent: NATO’s integrated air and missile defence, connecting sensors and effectors across the Allies; airborne early warning and control; a tanker fleet; dedicated suppression and stand-off capabilities; and fourth- and fifth-generation fighter fleets from Norway to Poland. Finland’s air force is built around dispersal—road bases, hardened shelters and rapid relocation—and received its first F-35As at Rovaniemi in late 2026, against an order of 64, with initial operational capability due in early 2028 and full capability by the end of 2030. Sweden brings its Gripen fleet and its own dispersed basing system. The same logic that makes Finnish and Baltic ground defence difficult to attack makes Allied air power difficult to destroy on the ground.

The geography compounds the problem rather than relieving it. Kaliningrad and the Leningrad Military District are enveloped, not enveloping; Russian airfields, headquarters and air-defence sites in the region lie within Allied strike range from several directions at once. Russian anti-access and area-denial capability is a claim to be tested rather than a fact to be conceded, and the Alliance has been testing it: Ramstein Flag 2026, flown across Europe from 8 to 18 June, exercised integrated air and missile defence, counter-A2AD tactics and agile combat employment, and Allied Air Command has since run counter-A2AD activity from the Baltic states to Romania under Eastern Sentry.

Nor has the air posture been standing still whilst the Lithuanian rotation was reviewed. Eastern Sentry was established in September 2025 after the Russian airspace violations of that month, adding fighters, helicopters, air-defence systems, surveillance aircraft and frigates along the eastern flank; by June 2026 Allied Air Command was describing it, without much ceremony, as the shift from an air policing mindset to an air defence mindset. At the Ankara summit on 8 July 2026 the Allies converted Baltic Air Policing itself—flown continuously since 30 March 2004—into an air defence mission, with engagement authority passing from national capitals to SACEUR and delegated through the Combined Air Operations Centre at Uedem. The precedents were already on the record: a Romanian F-16 destroyed a drone over Estonia on 19 May 2026, and a French Rafale another over Latvia on 8 June 2026, both on NATO’s authority rather than a capital’s.

With that established, the drone argument collapses of its own weight. A thousand drones a day is not a meteorological event. It requires launch sites, forward logistics, fuel, airframes, operators, communications relays and the reconnaissance to find targets—and a permissive corridor through which the whole apparatus can function. Every element of it is a target, and the corridor is precisely what NATO air and air-defence forces exist to deny. Ukraine absorbs waves of that kind today without air superiority, without airborne early warning, without a tanker fleet and whilst being bombed by an air force operating from sanctuary. The proposition that NATO, possessing all of those things, would be the party unable to cope has not been argued; it has merely been announced.

Air forces are not improvised at the moment of need, and NATO’s has been thirty years in the assembling. Everyone disregards the allied air forces at their peril.

7 - Cyber, drones and the force Russia would actually require

The invocation of ‘cyber’ is scarcely persuasive. Estonia has treated Russian cyber activity as a national-security threat since the coordinated attacks of 2007—long before much of the Alliance had learnt to spell ‘hybrid warfare’.
Tallinn hosts the NATO-accredited Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence, established in 2008. It develops doctrine, conducts technical and strategic research, trains Allied personnel and runs Locked Shields, the world’s largest live-fire cyber-defence exercise. The region has consequently been at the centre of hardening Allied networks, protecting critical infrastructure and developing the legal and operational framework for cyber defence.

From 2014 onwards, Ukrainian specialists trained and exchanged experience here. That relationship subsequently became reciprocal: Ukraine brought its hard-won operational knowledge of Russian intrusion, malware and attacks upon state and critical infrastructure back into the Allied system. Ukraine is now a contributing participant in the Tallinn Centre, and the exchange continues.

None of this makes Estonia invulnerable; no connected society is. It does, however, make the casual addition of ‘cyber’—as though NATO planners in Tallinn had never encountered a Russian keyboard—particularly fatuous. Cyberattack may disrupt systems and complicate mobilisation. It does not abolish geography, logistics, national resilience, Allied air and maritime power, or Russia’s need to assemble a visible invasion force.

Harping upon supposed Russian drone numbers proves nothing. NATO does not publicly disclose how many drones, interceptors, electronic-warfare systems, counter-UAS weapons or associated munitions are produced, procured, pre-positioned or operationally available across the theatre from Finland to Poland. Sushko does not possess those figures, and neither do the spectators confidently repeating his conclusion.

One cannot derive Allied incapacity from inventories one has never seen.

More importantly, Russia today possesses no identifiable follow-on force structure capable of conducting the operation being imagined here: a sustained combined-arms invasion of the Baltic states while still fighting Ukraine and simultaneously confronting NATO’s northern, central, air and maritime forces.

Such a campaign requires far more than drones, cyberattacks and an ominous thread on X. It requires trained and integrated manoeuvre formations; competent headquarters; engineers and bridging units; artillery, air defence and electronic warfare; enormous stocks of ammunition and fuel; protected logistics; medical support; aviation; reserves; and the capacity to replace losses while continuing the advance.

That force does not presently exist in the necessary structure and readiness. Reconstituting it would probably require at least another two years—and its creation could not be concealed. During precisely that period, Finnish, Estonian, Latvian, Lithuanian, Polish and wider Allied drone, interceptor, air-defence, fortification and mobilisation capabilities will not remain politely frozen at today’s level. They will continue to expand.

8 - Terrain, training and the fantasy of defeating NATO through morale

Finland is not an ornamental addition to NATO. It possesses a wartime strength of approximately 280,000 personnel, a trained reserve approaching 900,000, formidable artillery, dispersed aviation, prepared infrastructure and a society organised around comprehensive national defence. 

Kyrylo Budanov, speaking about Finnish volunteers in Ukraine, observed that Finnish fighters were markedly different from those of other countries and emphasised that most were ordinary Finnish reservists. The widely circulated English rendering—‘from another planet’—is looser than the original wording, but accurately conveys the respect behind the remark. So do the Russians understand what sort of soldiers the Finns are.

The Baltic states likewise train for the terrain they must defend: forests, wetlands, lakes, restricted roads, prepared obstacles, urban approaches and narrow manoeuvre corridors. These conditions do not make defence effortless, but they make glib extrapolation from the Ukrainian steppe militarily illiterate.

One fights a combined-arms war only as well as one has trained to fight it. NATO’s northern and Baltic forces repeatedly exercise mobilisation, reception of reinforcements, cross-border movement, fires, air operations, logistics, cyber defence and command integration. Russia cannot improvise the corresponding corps- and theatre-level competence by launching more drones.

Finnish and Baltic societies have lived beside Russia, under Soviet occupation or influenced by it, and facing Russian coercion for rather longer than most online commentators have studied them. Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Finland possess extensive reserve systems, civil preparedness, territorial defence, hardened infrastructure and plans for national resistance and mobilisation.

Finland’s famously ‘deadly aqua parks’ and Baltic ‘forests of death’ are jokes because the underlying preparations are decidedly not.

Could Russia attempt intimidation, cyberwarfare, sabotage or information operations? Of course. It already does. But suggesting that Baltic societies will simply lose heart and collapse before a ground campaign begins is neither evidence-based nor particularly respectful towards the people supposedly being defended.

The actual comparison

The Baltic states are not Ukraine in 2021–22. Ukraine then stood outside NATO. Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania are NATO Allies protected by Article 5, national mobilisation systems, regional defence plans, multinational forward formations, assigned reinforcement forces, Allied air and maritime components and the Joint Expeditionary Force.

Nor is closing a US embassy some ‘prerequisite’ Putin requires before invading. In Ukraine, the evacuation of diplomatic personnel followed months of visible Russian mobilisation and increasingly conclusive intelligence. Western military and intelligence services understood from autumn 2021 that Russia was preparing a major operation; by early December the direction of travel was evident, subsequent political temporising notwithstanding.

The embassy evacuation did not enable the invasion and did not predict it independently of that evidence. Cause and consequence have simply been reversed.

There is a historical absurdity here as well. The United States and Britain maintained the legal and diplomatic continuity of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania throughout fifty-one years of Soviet occupation. Today the United States operates substantial, security-conscious missions in Tallinn, Riga and Vilnius. Closing them is neither fashionable nor an item on Putin’s operational checklist.
Here in the Baltic states, governments, armed forces, intelligence services and Allied contingents maintain a sober view of what lies to our east. They watch, assess and understand material Russian movements. We can practically see them munching their dour kasha. We are neither blind nor asleep.

Prudence, preparation and vigilance are essential. So are stronger European stockpiles, better counter-drone capabilities, continued American engagement and seamless rotational handovers. But connecting unrelated facts with a red felt-tip pen is not strategic warning.
@vseviov, @Tsahkna, @John_ForemanCBE, @edwardlucas, @KeirGiles, @ChuckPfarrer and others are therefore right to urge calm, composure and focus. The purpose is to make deterrence sufficiently credible that kinetic defence never has to be tested.

Supporting Ukraine, strengthening the Baltic posture and preparing for real contingencies are serious work. Manufacturing an imaginary invasion countdown on social media is not.

The difficulty with signals and comments like @igorsushko is not merely the alarmism and evident lack of planning know-how. He plainly has not studied NATO’s actual force structure, the balance of air power over the theatre, Russia’s present capacity to generate a follow-on force, the terrain, the prepared defences, the reinforcement architecture or the political-military machinery of Article 5.

That is remediable. Genuinely have a look at the subject before announcing another Baltic invasion countdown. ‘Article 5 Under Stress and NATO’s Silver Lining’, published on 12 April 2026, sets out the two-wars framework, the obstruction playbook, the SACEUR problem and the constitutional limits on any American president who wished to obstruct. It was written in the spring, and it still holds. 
https://t.co/VmQx2IjMF6

We shall let you know when there is reason to shout. Until then: remain calm, remain vigilant and support Ukraine.

text:
This video has a talk by Laurence Moroney on how to get a job as an engineer in the age of AI, followed by what it means to be an engineer in the age of AI, but what caught my attention is the comments about "hard work". In the introduction to Laurence Moroney's talk, Andrew Ng says (I'm going to take the trouble to quote this):

"I'm going to say one last thing that is considered not politically correct in some circles. But but I'll just say it anyway, which is in some circles it has become considered not politically correct to encourage others to work hard. I'm going to encourage you to work hard. Now I think the reason some people don't like that is because there are some people, they're in a phase of life where they're not in a position to work hard. So right after my children were born, I was not working hard for a short period of time. And there are people because of an injury, disability, whatever -- very valid reasons -- they're not in a position to work hard at that moment in time and we should respect them support them make sure they're well taken care of even though they're not working hard. Having said that, all of my PhD students that became very successful, I saw every single one of them work incredibly hard. The 2 am setting up hyperparameter tuning, you know, been there, done that, right? Still doing it some days. If you are fortunate enough to be in a position in life where you can work really hard, there are so many opportunities to do things right now. If you get excited, as I do, spending evenings and weekends coding and building stuff, and getting user feedback, if you lean in and do those things, it will increase your odds of being really successful. So, I don't know, maybe I'll get in some trouble with some people, encouraging you to work hard, but I find that the truth is people that work hard get a lot more done. We should also respect people that don't and people that aren't in a position to do so. But between watching some dumb TV show versus finding your agentic coder on a weekend to try something. I'm going to choose the latter almost every time."

Then in the Laurence Moroney's talk itself, he says: 

"Andrew said something politically incorrect earlier on. I'm going to also say a similar politically incorrect thing. First of all, hard work. Hard work is such a nebulous term that I would say that I think about hard work in terms of: you are what you measure. There is the whole trend out there. I'm trying to remember. Was it 996 or is it 669? 996, right? 9:00 am to 900 pm six days a week, is a metric of hard work. It's not. That's not a metric of hard work. That's a metric of time spent. I would encourage everybody, in the same way as Andrew did, to think about hard work, but what hard work is, is how you measure that hard work. You can work eight hours a day and be incredibly productive. You can work six hours a day and be incredibly productive. But it's the metric of how hard you work and how you measure that. I personally measure that from output, things that I have created in the time that I spent. I joke a lot, but it's true, that I've written a lot of books. Andrew held up one -- that one that he held up -- that he helped me write a little bit. I actually wrote that book in about two months. And people say, how how do you have time with your jobs and all these kind of things? How do you do this? You must work, like, 16 hours a day in order to be able to do this? But actually, the key to me being able to write books is baseball. Any baseball fans here? I love baseball, but if you sit down and try to watch baseball on TV, a match can take like three and a half or four hours. So, all of my writing I tend to do in baseball season. So, I'm like if I'm going to sit down, I like the Mariners, I'm from Seattle. I like the Dodgers. Nobody booed. Okay, good. And you know, so like usually one of those is going to be playing at 7:00 at night. So, instead of sitting in front of the TV just like watching baseball mindlessly, I'll actually be writing a book while baseball's on in the background. It's a very slowmoving game. This is something like that's the hard work, you know, in this case. And I would encourage you to try to find areas where you can work hard and produce output. And that's the second pillar here -- is that business focus."

What's all this about "hard work" suddenly becoming "politically correct" all about?

I'll tell you what I think it is. One time in the last few months I came across some people on Hacker News talking about how "997"-in-office (not remote) was now the standard job offer for a software engineer in Silicon Valley. I have to say up front that I don't know if this is true or not. Maybe a handful of employers are offering "997" jobs, and maybe a handful of people who applied for those people are talking about it on HN. Or maybe all employers are offering "997" jobs and it's the only thing on offer for software engineers. (The term "997" is a variation on "996", as Laurence Moroney mentioned, and comes from China where 9:00am to 9:00pm, 6 days/week is considered the standard software engineer work day at major companies like Alibaba.) I don't know, I don't have any sense of proportion. But they were saying, with all the layoffs, software engineers lost their leverage, so now, if an employer offers you a "997" job and you don't take it, there's thousands of people in line right behind you who will take it.

But here's the catch: I learned when I was in my 20s that a 23-year-old software engineer will last, on average, 2.5 years working 80 hours/week. I worked 80-hour weeks for 5 years starting when I was 23. The 2.5 year figure came from a woman who worked in the HR department of a major tech company. The company's hiring policy was to hire only new college graduates for software engineering jobs (with exceptions made for people who were famous for doing something brilliant and hired into high-level positions), work them 80 hours/week, and when they burned out, to hire more. (I later learned that the term "burn out" has 2 meanings: one is, physical exhaustion, and the other is, to lose enthusiasm for whatever you're working on. I'm talking here only about the first meaning. A person who is physically exhausted from working 80-hour weeks for years cannot regain their energy by switching to a different job, one that they will have more "enthusiasm" for. A person who is "burned out" in the physical exhaustion sense cannot work. They either voluntarily stop working and rest and recover, or they are forced to stop working by getting fired, either for illness or just unacceptably low productivity.) The HR person said 2.5 years is the "half-life" of software engineer productivity when working 80 hours/week starting around age 23.

Well, if there's any truth to the "997" claim, if you do the math, 9:00am to 9:00pm is 12 hours, and for 7 days a week, 12 x 7 = 84. So "997" is an 84-hour workweek. So, rumor has it that in Silicon Valley, the standard job offer for software engineers now is an 84-hour workweek.

If that's true, or even just mostly true if not entirely true, then these Stanford students have good reason to feel fear when they hear the words "hard work".

Andrew Ng and Laurence Moroney seems to simultaneously be trying to tell these students to buckle down and accept the "hard work" they have to do, while simultaneously trying to weasel out of what "hard work" means. Andrew Ng talks about "getting excited spending evenings and weekends coding and building stuff, and getting user feedback." There's a big difference between doing something you feel excited about and something an employer dictated you have to do. If you're just doing stuff because you feel excited about, when you feel tired you can rest. If your employer dictates you work "997", when you feel tired, you don't get to rest, you have to keep working. You have to override your body's need for rest, and that's what leads you to that 2.5 year burnout. Andrew Ng is so famous no employer has the leverage to make him work "997" so it's a non-issue for him, he can work hard when he feels excited and rest when he feels tired, but the same isn't true of low-level people newly hired into tech companies. Laurence Moroney seems to weasel out by saying it's not the time spent, it's what you measure. Measure what's important, and you can be productive in 8 hours or even 6 hours per day. You can write books with baseball on in the background. As general life advice that might be all right, but if your employer is requiring "997" and it's "in office" (not remote), then you have to be physically present in the office and working -- you are being watched to make sure you are working the entire time -- then you really do have to work the 12 hours/day, 7 days/week. You can't weasel out of it by saying, oh, I'm being smart about what I measure.

Also, if you're thinking, the companies must be violating some labor law, they have to pay overtime, or somesuch, at least when I lived in California, unless the laws have changed since then, there's a special exception in the laws for tech workers so salaried tech workers don't have any limit on work hours and there is no overtime requirement or anything. Maybe if they were in your state, there would be some law. But this talk is being given at Stanford University which is in the San Francisco Bay Area (aka Silicon Valley) in California.

If any of you are out in California and getting "997" job offers, my advice is: think seriously about whether you can get seriously rich (for example from stock options) in 2.5 years, give or take. If you can make a huge amount of money very fast, if you can end up "set for life", or nearly so, the "hard work" might be worth it. If you can't, or it's too big a gamble, it might not be worth burning yourself out (in the exhaustion sense of the term) on it. Your decision, of course, but I think these are the terms in which you should think about the cost-benefit tradeoff.

I know a lot of people in software in Silicon Valley are thinking they need to get a job at a top company or top AI lab to escape the "permanent underclass", which is what they believe will happen to everyone that does not make enough money before AI automates the jobs and they all disappear.

https://t.co/senLGcB06E

The term "permanent underclass" came out in a New York Times article that came out about 3 months ago. The NY Times article is paywalled for me, but I saw this interview of the author, Jasmine Sun, on Taylor Lorenz's YouTube channel.

It's a long video (51 minutes), and I ended up not doing a separate post about it because I felt like 51 minutes was a bit to much to ask anyone to watch. At one point, during the discussion, I felt like the whole discussion was missing a timeframe. By which I mean, if the timeframe is short, like say, "6 months", then, yes, worrying about falling into the "permanent underclass" does seem hyperbolic. If the timeframe is long, say 20 years, then worrying about falling into the "permanent underclass" does not seem hyperbolic. It seems likely AI will have automated all jobs in 20 years. Maybe 25 -- not that much in the grand scheme of things. The true time frame that is actually going to happen is probably somewhere in between -- more than 6 months, less than 20 years. If you aspire to escape the "permanent underclass", then the better you can calibrate, the better.

https://t.co/5w3piJPANc

Related: I didn't use the term "permanent underclass" in this "conversation with AI", but if you're interested in the moral landscape of what a world with a "permanent underclass" might look like with or without universal basic income (UBI), you might want to check it out.

BREAKING: Journalist and college professor Stacey Patton goes viral by penning a stunningly powerful statement about how she was on Charlie Kirk’s “digital hit list” and recounting the horror that he inflicted on her.

We cannot allow this tragic assassination to whitewash Kirk’s legacy…

“I am on Charlie Kirk’s hit list,” Patton wrote to her 215,000 followers on Facebook. “His so-called ‘Professor Watchlist,’ run under the umbrella of Turning Point USA, is nothing more than a digital hit list for academics who dare to speak truth to power. I landed there in 2024 after writing commentary that inflamed the MAGA faithful. And once my name went up, the harassment machine roared to life.”

“For weeks my inbox and voicemail were deluged. Mostly white men spat venom through the phone: ‘bitch,’ ‘c*nt,’ ‘n****r.’ They threatened all manner of violence,” she continued.

“They overwhelmed the university’s PR lines and the president’s office with calls demanding that I be fired,” Patton wrote. “The flood was so relentless that the head of campus security reached out to offer me an escort, because they feared one of these keyboard soldiers might step out of his basement and come do me harm.”

“And I am not unique,” she added.

“Kirk’s Watchlist has terrorized legions of professors across this country. Women, Black faculty, queer scholars, basically anyone who challenged white supremacy, gun culture, or Christian nationalism suddenly found themselves targets of coordinated abuse,” Patton wrote.

“Some received death threats. Some had their jobs threatened. Some left academia entirely. Kirk sent the loud message to us: speak the truth and we will unleash the mob!” she continued.

“That is the culture of violence Charlie Kirk built. He normalized violence.  He curated it, monetized it, and sicced it on anyone who dared to puncture his movement’s lies,” she wrote.

“And now, in the wake of his shooting, there’s all this national outpouring of mourning, moments of silence, yellow prayer hands, and tributes painting him as a civil debater,” Patton continued. “But the truth is that Kirk and his foot soldiers spent years terrorizing educators, trying to silence us with harassment and fear!”

“And now the same violence he unleashed on others has come full circle.”

“But what i find especially jarring is the dissonance in public mourning for a smug white man whose life work was actively hostile to certain groups,” she continued. “Kirk spent years demonizing LGBTQ people, mocking gun survivors, spewing racism about Black folks, and pushing policies that literally shorten lives.”

“It is so revolting to watch a bipartisan wave of grief sweep over this hateful racist as if he was a neutral community servant,” she concluded.

This is pure unvarnished truth from Patton. Charlie Kirk did not deserve what happened to him, but nor did his victims deserve the hell that he unleashed on them. If Americans are going to build a more peaceful future for ourselves we must condemn political violence while also condemning the hateful, bigoted rhetoric that made Kirk a multimillionaire. 

Please retweet and ❤️ if Patton’s message struck a chord with you!
